memory_candidates.content: PyMuPDF page.insert_text(point, text, fontsize=n) does NOT wrap. A single line whose rendered width exceeds the page's usable width (page width minus the x-origin, e.g. ~540pt on a 612pt-wide US-letter page starting at x=72) is silently truncated mid-word on extraction -- no exception, no return-value signal distinguishable from a normal single-line insert (insert_text returns 1 in both the truncated and non-truncated single-line case in this PyMuPDF version). This can silently corrupt a hermetic PDF fixture's intended text content (e.g. clipping the very sentence-fusion boundary a regression test is trying to construct) with no visible failure until the extracted text is inspected. General lesson: for any PDF-fixture line built with insert_text() (not insert_textbox(), which does wrap), keep it well under ~70-90 characters at 10pt body-text sizes, or verify the round-trip through get_text() rather than trusting the source string literal's full content survived.

When re-running an offline regex/text-analysis check against a corpus directory's on-disk markdown for read-only acceptance verification, do not assume a single non-chunked {doc_id}.md file still exists -- a downstream RAG/embedding pipeline may have replaced it with overlapping chunk_NNNN.md fragments, each carrying a per-chunk citation header line prepended to its body text. Naively concatenating such fragment files with no separator (e.g. `text += open(f).read()`) glues the end of one fragment directly onto the next fragment's header line with no intervening whitespace, fabricating spurious zero-space-transition hits that look identical to the real defect signature a check like this is trying to measure. Join fragments with a blank line (or otherwise insert a separator) before running any pattern that is sensitive to word/sentence-boundary whitespace, and re-derive raw counts fresh rather than trusting a prior research pass's cached numbers to still be reproducible via the same method.
